source_text: Ἀλλὰ γὰρ ὁ μὲν περὶ τοῦ δυνατὴν εἶναι τὴν τῆς σαρκὸς ἀνάστασιν ἱκανῶς ἀποδέδεικταί μοι λόγος κατὰ τοὺς ἐθνικούς. Eἰ δὲ κατὰ τοὺς ἀπίστους οὐχ εὑρίσκεται ἀδύνατος ἡ ἀνάστασις τῆς σαρκός, πόσῳ μᾶλλον κατὰ τοὺς πιστούς! Ἑξῆς δὲ λεκτέον πρὸς τοὺς ἀτιμάζοντας τὴν σάρκα καὶ φάσκοντας μὴ ἀξίαν εἶναι τῆς ἀναστάσεως μηδὲ τῆς ἐπουρανίου πολιτείας· ὅτι πρῶτον αὐτῆς ἐστιν ἡ οὐσία γῆ, μετέπειτα δὲ καὶ μεστὴ γέγονε πάσης ἁμαρτίας, ὥστε καὶ τὴν ψυχὴν ἀναγκάσαι συναμαρτάνειν. Ἐοίκασι δὲ οὗτοι τὴν ὅλην τοῦ θεοῦ πραγματείαν ἀγνοεῖν, καὶ τὴν ἐξ ἀρχῆς γένεσιν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου καὶ πλάσιν, καὶ τὰ ἐν κόσμῳ ὧν ἕνεκα γέγονεν. Ἢ γὰρ οὔ φησιν ὁ λόγος· Ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον κατ' εἰκόνα ἡμετέραν καὶ καθ' ὁμοίωσιν; Ποῖον; Σαρκικὸν δῆλον ὅτι λέγει ἄνθρωπον. Φησὶ γὰρ ὁ λόγος· Καὶ ἔλαβεν ὁ θεὸς χοῦν ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς καὶ ἔπλασε τὸν ἄνθρωπον. ∆ῆλον οὖν ὡς κατ' εἰκόνα θεοῦ πλασσόμενος ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἦν σαρκικός. Eἶτα πῶς οὐκ ἄτοπον τὴν ὑπὸ θεοῦ σάρκα πλασθεῖσαν κατ' εἰκόνα τὴν ἑαυτοῦ φάσκειν ἄτιμον εἶναι καὶ οὐδενὸς ἀξίαν; Ὅτι δὲ τίμιον κτῆμα ἡ σὰρξ παρὰ θεῷ δῆλον πρῶτον μὲν ἐκ τοῦ πρὸς αὐτοῦ πεπλᾶσθαι, εἴ γε καὶ εἰκὼν τῷ πλάστῃ καὶ ζωγράφῳ τιμία γινομένη· καὶ ἐκ τῆς λοιπῆς δὲ κοσμοποιΐας μαθεῖν πάρεστιν· οὗ γὰρ ἕνεκεν γέγονε τὰ λοιπά, τοῦτο πάντων τῷ ποιήσαντι τιμιώτατον.
pass_a_gloss: But indeed the argument that the resurrection of the body is possible has been sufficiently demonstrated to me against the Gentiles. But if the resurrection of the body is not found to be impossible even against the unbelievers, how much more so against the believers! Next, it should be said to those who dishonor the body and claim it is not worthy of resurrection or of the heavenly citizenship, that first its substance is earth, and afterwards it has become full of all sin, so that it even forces the soul to sin together with it. These people seem to be ignorant of the whole work of God, and of the original creation and formation of man, and of the things in the world for which he was made. For does not the Word say, 'Let us make man in our image and according to our likeness?' What kind of man is it clear that it speaks of? It is clear that it speaks of a fleshly man. For the Word says, 'And God took dust from the earth and formed man.' It is clear, therefore, that man was fleshly when he was formed in the image of God. Then how is it not absurd to claim that the body, which was formed by God in His own image, is dishonorable and worthy of nothing? That the body is a valuable possession from God is clear, first from the fact that it was formed by Him, if indeed even the image of the Creator and Artist becomes valuable; and it is also possible to learn from the rest of creation, for that for which the other things were made is the most valuable of all to the One who made them.

choices.why: describing something as unworthy of respect

bible_refs.note: Let us make man in our image and according to our likeness

pass_b_english: I have, in fact, already demonstrated sufficiently to the Gentiles that the resurrection of the body is possible. But if the resurrection of the body is not found impossible even in the judgment of unbelievers, how much more impossible must it be in the judgment of believers! Next, we must answer those who dishonor the body and assert that it is unworthy of the resurrection or of the heavenly citizenship. They argue that its substance is first of all earth, and that afterwards it has become full of all sin, so that it even compels the soul to sin along with it. These people appear to be ignorant of the whole work of God, of the original creation and formation of man, and of the things in the world for the sake of which he was made. For does the Word not say, 'Let us make man in our image, according to our likeness' (Genesis 1:26)? What kind of man does it clearly speak of? It clearly speaks of a fleshly man. For the Word says, 'And God took dust from the earth and formed man.' It is clear, therefore, that man was fleshly when he was formed in the image of God. Then how is it not absurd to claim that the flesh, formed by God in His own image, is dishonorable and worthy of nothing? That the flesh is a valuable possession with God is clear, first, from its having been formed by Him, if indeed even the image of the Creator and Artist becomes valuable; and it is also possible to learn this from the rest of creation. For that for the sake of which the other things were made is the most valuable of all to the One who made them.

review.notes: The translation accurately reflects the Greek text. Pass B correctly identifies and adds the scripture citation (Genesis 1:26) for the quoted phrase 'Ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον κατ' εἰκόνα ἡμετέραν καὶ καθ' ὁμοίωσιν'. Pass A and B both preserve the nuances of the argument regarding the body's substance and its value to the Creator.
